summaries.gardner: Phillips 66 is the opposite of a Rule Breaker: it is a mature refiner, pipeline and chemicals company in a shrinking-to-flat fuels market, not the top dog of an emerging industry. The one Rule Breaker trait it shows is strong recent momentum (up about 126% over 52 weeks to $293.17), driven by commodity margins rather than innovation.
summaries.buffett: Buffett would see an understandable business with valuable hard assets, a 50% chemicals stake and steady buybacks (diluted shares down from 473.7M in 2022 to 402.6M in Q2 2026), but no durable pricing power and highly cyclical earnings (a $3,975M loss in 2020, $11,024M profit in 2022, $2,117M in 2024). At about 16.7x trailing earnings and 3.7x book after the 2026 spike, there is little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the simplicity and the irreplaceable nature of permitted refineries and pipelines, but would note that a commodity business with weak pricing power, heavy capital needs and debt of $20,565M is not the kind of great business he preferred. Inverting, the main ways to lose are a collapse in crack spreads and long-term fuel-demand decline.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms Phillips 66 is a cyclical, and the 2026 crack-spread boom (Q2 2026 adjusted EPS $9.41 vs $2.38 a year earlier) looks like late-cycle peak earnings, when cyclicals look cheapest on forward P/E (about 9-10x) yet are riskiest. Analysts expect revenue and earnings to fall in 2027-2028, so the P/E-to-growth test fails.
summaries.fisher: Fisher's growth criteria fit poorly: sales have fallen three years in a row to $132,376M in 2025, R&D is small, and the company's edge is operational, not new products. Management has improved its focus (asset sales, EPIC NGL acquisition), but growth depends on commodity markets.
summaries.graham: Phillips 66 passes Graham's size and dividend-continuity basics only partly: it is large, but it has paid dividends only since its 2012 spin-off, lost money in 2020, and trades near 28x average 2023-2025 EPS and about 3.7x book, far above Graham's 15x and 22.5 limits. EPS did grow about 40% from $7.73 (2015) to $10.79 (2025).
summaries.thiel: Phillips 66 answers few of Thiel's questions: it has no proprietary technology 10x better than rivals, competes in a crowded commodity market with Marathon, Valero and the majors, and has no monopoly. Its durable assets and distribution network are real but not a zero-to-one opportunity.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable compounders riding secular trends with efficient operations; Phillips 66 is a cyclical, capital-intensive refiner whose recent surge comes from commodity margins. Its cost cuts and buybacks show some fitness, but revenue is expected to fall in 2027-2028.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller would focus on the liquidity and the margin cycle: the 2026 supply shock lifted refining margins to $24.08/bbl in Q2 2026 and earnings estimates rose, which suited a momentum trade, but consensus already expects 2027 revenue and EPS to decline. The 18-24 month outlook is for normalization, not further acceleration.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith's tests (high returns on capital, high gross margins, cash conversion, no cyclicality) are mostly failed: gross margin after crude costs was about 12% in 2025, returns swing with the cycle, and the business is heavily exposed to commodity prices. It is not a Fundsmith-style quality company.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Phillips 66's trailing earnings yield (EBIT of about $10.0B over EV of about $133B, roughly 7.5%) is moderate, and return on capital is around 12% on the latest twelve months but much lower in 2024. It would rank middling, flattered by cyclical 2026 earnings.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs an exceptional business, talented and honest management and good reinvestment opportunities; Phillips 66 has competent management and some midstream reinvestment, but the core refining business is cyclical with weak pricing power, so it fails the first leg.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks simple businesses in temporary distress bought at deep discounts; Phillips 66 is simple to understand but is now priced near a 52-week high after a 126% gain, so the low-risk, high-uncertainty setup has passed.
summaries.wood: Phillips 66 sits outside ARK's innovation platforms: it refines fossil fuels, and its renewable diesel plant is a conventional conversion rather than a disruptive technology with falling cost curves. Wood would more likely see it as a business exposed to disruption from electrification.
summaries.ackman: Ackman wants simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and pricing power; Phillips 66 is simple and generated $6,394M of trailing free cash flow, but it is cyclical and lacks pricing power. Elliott's 2025 activist campaign shows the activist angle, but it is not an Ackman-style quality compounder.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economies-shared model does not fit: Phillips 66 does not pass scale savings to customers to build an ever-stronger moat, and its long-term position in fuels is likely weaker, not stronger. Its strengths are asset scale and integration, not a customer-flywheel.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge, growing markets with a technical breakthrough; Phillips 66 is a 2012 spin-off of an old oil company in a mature market, so it fits none of his criteria.
summaries.nash: Under Tom Nash's process Phillips 66 fails key screens: it is a commodity producer, has more debt ($20,565M) than cash ($4,099M), an operating margin near 5-6%, falling multi-year revenue, and a DCF value far below the $293.17 price. Its strengths are a long history, strong recent earnings beats and very low short interest (1.38%), giving a Nash score of about 65.

momentum.evidence: The shares closed at $293.17 on Oct 16, 2026, up about 126% over 52 weeks and about 54% over six months, far ahead of the market.

g4.evidence: Chairman and CEO Mark Lashier is an experienced engineer-executive, and Elliott Management (nearly 6% stake in 2025) won two board seats, but there is no famous long-term backer.

g6.evidence: After the 2026 rally some analysts see it as fully valued (consensus target about $280 vs a $293 price, Mizuho downgrade to neutral), but most still rate it Buy.

simple.evidence: It refines crude into fuels, sells them through Phillips 66, 76 and Conoco brands, and earns fees from pipelines and NGL fractionation: a business a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Results swing widely: net income attributable was -$3,975M in 2020, $11,024M in 2022, $2,117M in 2024 and $4,403M in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Management returns cash (2025 dividends $1,922M and buybacks $1,207M) and sold non-core assets, but shareholders split board seats 2-2 with Elliott in May 2025 over performance and governance, including the combined chair/CEO role.

b6.evidence: It resisted Elliott's breakup plan and kept integration, and it bought EPIC NGL and the rest of WRB Refining, which are logical extensions rather than empire building, though the 2025 fight centred on this question.

roic.evidence: Return on capital is cyclical: about 12% over the last twelve months but much lower in 2024 when net income was only $2,117M on equity of about $28.5B, and the balance sheet carries $20,565M of debt.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capital spending) was positive in 2021-2025, e.g. $2,729M in 2025 vs net income of $4,403M, and $6,394M over the last twelve months, but it was -$809M in 2020.

b10.evidence: Book equity and the share price have both risen since the 2012 spin-off, but much of the recent gain comes from the 2026 margin spike, so retained-earnings value creation is hard to separate from the cycle.

safety.evidence: A Nash-style DCF on 3-year average FCF margin of about 2.3% gives a value far below the $293.17 price, and the stock trades at about 3.7x book value.

fairprice.evidence: About 9-10x 2026-2027 consensus EPS ($32.17 and $29.76) looks cheap, but those are peak-cycle earnings; at 16.7x trailing and 28x average 2023-2025 EPS it is not cheap.

mu5.evidence: Diversification across midstream, chemicals and marketing lowers failure risk, but a crack-spread collapse, EV-driven demand decline or tighter regulation could sharply cut earnings.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in NGL midstream (Zeus gas plant, new Coastal Bend fractionator) and chemicals (Golden Triangle Polymers, Ras Laffan, due 2027), but refining offers few high-return growth projects.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic cyclical: earnings rise and fall with refining crack spreads and chemical margins.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E is about 16.7, while analysts expect EPS to fall from about $32 in 2026 to about $30 in 2027, so the P/E is far above the growth rate.

runway.evidence: Consensus expects revenue to fall from about $172B in 2026 to $147B by 2028, and US fuel demand is mature.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 473.7M in 2022 to 402.6M in Q2 2026 through buybacks, but insiders have been sellers (CFO Kevin Mitchell sold 29,400 shares at $170 in May 2026).

ly8.evidence: It is a large, widely covered S&P 500 company with about 80% institutional ownership and roughly 20 analysts.

fi2.evidence: It converted the Rodeo refinery to renewable fuels (about 50,000 b/d) and is expanding NGL and polymers capacity, but fuels remain its core product.

fi3.evidence: Research spending is small, and its main new-product bet, Renewable Fuels, lost $380M pre-tax in 2025.

fi4.evidence: It has a large branded network of about 7,620 US outlets, but fuel sales are driven by price and location rather than salesmanship.

longterm.evidence: Management argues for long-term integrated value (midstream and chemicals growth) against Elliott's breakup push, but it also emphasizes near-term cost cuts and shareholder returns.

gr1.evidence: It had $132,376M of 2025 sales and a market value of about $117B.

ni10.evidence: It lost $3,975M attributable to Phillips 66 in 2020.

gr4.evidence: It has paid dividends only since its 2012 spin-off from ConocoPhillips, about 14 years.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $7.73 in 2015 to $10.79 in 2025, about 40%.

gr6.evidence: At $293.17 it trades at about 28x average 2023-2025 diluted EPS of $10.42.

gr7.evidence: Trailing P/E of about 16.7 times price-to-book of about 3.7 gives about 62, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its refining, pipeline and chemical technology is standard industry practice, not 10x better than rivals.

timing.evidence: 2026 timing is favourable for refining margins after the Middle East supply shock, but long-term timing for fossil fuels is unfavourable.

th3.evidence: It started as a large share of a large, mature market (spun off in 2012 as a major US refiner).

team.evidence: Mark Lashier is a capable engineer-CEO with chemicals experience, but not an exceptional founder, and his record drew an activist challenge in 2025.

th5.evidence: It has an established distribution network: about 70,000 miles of pipelines and about 7,620 branded US outlets.

durable.evidence: Pipelines, NGL hubs and chemicals should endure for decades, but refining and gasoline face long-term decline from electrification and efficiency.

th7.evidence: Its strategy (integrated refining, NGL midstream and chemicals) is shared by many rivals.

trend.evidence: It is not a beneficiary of AI or cloud; its exposure to the energy trend is to fossil fuels and NGLs.

dr1.evidence: Earnings accelerated in 2026 (Q2 adjusted EPS $9.41 vs $2.38) and estimates rose, but consensus expects 2027 EPS ($29.76) below 2026 ($32.17).

dr2.evidence: Consensus expects 2027-2028 revenue and earnings to fall as crack spreads normalize.

dr4.evidence: Tight fuel markets favour it now, but a weaker economy would hurt fuel demand and margins, and its $20.6B debt is sensitive to rates.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include Q3 2026 results on Oct 28, 2026 and the 2027 start-up of the Golden Triangle and Ras Laffan polymer plants, but they are mostly known.

dr7.evidence: Commodity exposure and cyclical earnings make it unsuitable for a large, concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Sales minus purchased crude and products were about 12.3% of sales in 2025.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $6.4B gives a yield of about 5.5% on a $117B market cap, but normal-year FCF (e.g. $2,729M in 2025) gives only about 2.3%.

gb2.evidence: Trailing EBIT of about $10.0B (pre-tax income plus interest) is about 7.5% of an enterprise value of about $133B.

pa2.evidence: The industry is in a cyclical upswing in 2026, not a temporary setback.

pa4.evidence: Its diversified assets make permanent loss of the business unlikely, but buying after a 126% one-year rise at peak margins risks large losses if margins revert.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Its unit costs are not falling rapidly with volume; refining is a mature-cost business.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its fuels and NGL markets are mature and will not grow many times over in five years.

ac3.evidence: Its earnings depend heavily on crude, product and chemical prices: refining pre-tax income swung from $5,340M in 2023 to -$274M in 2025.

ns1.evidence: It sells at market prices and does not pass scale savings to customers to build a moat.

ns4.evidence: Its 10-20 year position in refining is likely weaker as fuel demand declines, though midstream may hold up.

va2.evidence: Reliable fuel and NGL supply solves an important problem, but many suppliers solve it equally well.

tn1.evidence: It is an old fossil-fuel business, not one built for a secular trend; renewable diesel is a retrofit of the Rodeo refinery.

tn2.evidence: The market sees it as a refiner, while it is gradually becoming more of an NGL midstream and chemicals company, but the gap is modest.

tn3.evidence: It is a commodity processor exposed to commodity prices, a zone Nash avoids.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable (TTM net income about $7.1B) and TTM sales are up, but annual revenue fell in 2023-2025 and debt of $20,565M far exceeds cash of $4,099M.

tn5.evidence: Q1 2026 operating cash flow was -$2,264M (negative free cash flow) and debt exceeded cash in every recent quarter.

tn6.evidence: Last-twelve-month sales of $152,167M are about 15% above FY2025, but FY2025 revenue fell 7.5% and analysts expect declines in 2027-2028.

tn7.evidence: About 15% revenue growth plus a roughly 4% FCF margin is about 19, well below 40.

tn8.evidence: Trailing-twelve-month total revenues and other income rose about 14.5% vs FY2025 while total costs and expenses rose about 12.5%.

tn9.evidence: It fails several instant kills: debt exceeds cash and operating margin is about 5-6%, far below 20%.

tn10.evidence: There is no single existential legal threat, but it faces ongoing environmental regulation, California fuel policy and renewable-fuel credit rules.

tn11.evidence: It provides refined fuels, NGL services and petrochemical feedstocks that help drivers, airlines and industry get reliable energy, and charges market prices for products plus fees for pipelines and fractionation.

tn13.evidence: Score about 65 of 130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 5, operating margin 0, short interest 10, institutional ownership 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 10, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 0, secular trend 0, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in 2023-2025, margins did not expand steadily, free cash flow was -$809M in 2020 and fell from $8,619M (2022) to $2,729M (2025), and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 8.7x (TTM pre-tax income plus interest of $10,037M over $1,154M interest), current ratio 1.32 and liabilities 1.5x equity pass, but assets excluding goodwill ($80,377M) are only 1.64x liabilities ($49,107M).

tn18.evidence: Lashier has been CEO only since July 2022, is not a founder, and no open-market purchases were found, while other insiders have sold.

tn20.evidence: It beat consensus EPS in each of the last five quarters (Q2 2025 to Q2 2026, e.g. $9.41 vs $7.50 in Q2 2026) but missed in Q1 2025.

tn21.evidence: No accounting or fraud concerns are known, but it has made several acquisitions (EPIC NGL, WRB stake), margins are cyclical, and insiders sold into the 2026 rally.

tn22.evidence: It has large real revenue ($132,376M in 2025), is profitable, shrinks its share count through buybacks and is not a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: A $117B market cap against normal-year free cash flow of about $2.7B (2025) implies strong growth, while revenue has been falling.

tn25.evidence: With 3-year average revenue growth of about -8% and FCF margin of about 2.3%, a 12% discount rate and 4% terminal growth, value per share is well under $50, far below $293.17.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 9-10x is in line with refining peers, but 2027 EPS is expected to fall below 2026, so there is no PEG at or below 1.
